questions.question_text: Which of the following subtests of Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS) is noted to resist any decline with aging?
questions.explanation:
Hold tests are supposed to be resistant to age-related decline; so they may be sensitive to organic brain damage such as dementia. The current version of Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS-IV) yields an overall IQ score, plus four index scores and scores on component subtests including: Verbal Comprehension Scale (similarities, vocabulary, information, comprehension); Perceptual Reasoning Scale (block design, matrix reasoning, visual puzzles, picture completion, figure weights); Working Memory Scale (digit span, arithmetic, letter-number sequencing); Processing Speed Scale (symbol search, coding, cancellation).
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Hayling test in neuropsychological assessments is used to test which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Failures in semantic inhibition are frequently measured with the Hayling Sentence Completion test. In the Hayling test, the individual is presented with 30 sentences where the last word is missing. In the first 15 sentences (Automatic section), the word is strongly cued by the preceding context, and the individual must complete the sentence by producing the missing word. In the next 15 sentences (Inhibition section), a word that makes no sense in the sentence context or is unrelated to the target word must be given by the individual. Thus, in order to complete the sentence, the individual has to inhibit the automatic response and generate a new unrelated word.
Ref: Cervera-Crespo T, González-Alvarez J. Age and semantic inhibition measured by the hayling task: a meta-analysis. Archives of Clinical Neuropsychology. 2017 Mar 1;32(2):198-214.

questions.question_text: A 49-year-old patient with schizophrenia scored poorly on Brixton test. This shows deficits in
questions.explanation:
The Brixton Spatial Anticipation Test is a well-established test of executive function that evaluates the capacity to abstract, follow, and switch rules. It bears similarities to the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, in that it evaluates the ability to acquire and follow rules, to switch between rules, and to inhibit earlier response patterns. It makes minimal verbal demands. The test consists of 10 numbered circles, one of which is coloured blue. The participant is required to anticipate the position of the blue circle on each successive page of a 55-page test booklet by identifying patterns that vary over the course of the task. Thus, it is a visuospatial sequencing task that measures the ability to learn rules from sequences of stimuli. It is often used to assess executive functioning in people with neurological disorders such as strokes, dementia, and psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia.
Ref: Rao SP et al. Distinct performance profiles on the Brixton test in frontotemporal dementia. Journal of Neuropsychology. 2021 Jun;15(2):162-85.

questions.question_text: During extended cognitive assessment by a neuropsychologist, the subject is asked to read a short story containing 25 elements and the psychologist tested both immediate and delayed recall after 30 minutes. The test done by the neuropsychologist is called
questions.explanation: Here the subject is asked to read a short story from the Wechsler Memory scale containing 25 elements and both immediate and delayed recall after an interval of 30 minutes is tested. This is one of the verbal subtests used in Wechsler memory scale. WMS-3 consists of tests grouped under two domains; verbal and nonverbal, all of which have immediate and delayed recall and or recognition components. It also has a third group of tests involve .mental control subtests'.

questions.question_text: A psychologist is performing neuropsychological testing in a 45 year old man. Which one of the following is a test of set shifting?
questions.explanation:
The Wisconsin card sorting task is a test of frontal lobe functioning. The patient has to determine the rule for card allocation and allocate cards accordingly. When the rule changes, a patient with frontal lobe dysfunction is likely to make more errors (tests response inhibition and set shifting).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 88.

questions.question_text: Transcriptome is a
questions.explanation: A transcriptome is different from a genome, the latter being the entire DNA sequence of an organism. A transcriptome represents the very small percentage of the genome - less than 5 percent in humans - that is transcribed into RNA molecules. A gene may produce many different types of mRNA molecules, so a transcriptome is much more complex than the genome that encodes it.

questions.question_text: A nonsense mutation refers to
questions.explanation:
A nonsense mutation is any mutation that produces one of the stop codons, causing premature termination of protein synthesis by the gene in which it occurs.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: The gene most strongly implicated in ADHD is
questions.explanation:
Family studies and population-based studies have found an association between the dopamine 4 receptor seven-repeat allele (DRD4) gene and ADHD.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 139.

questions.question_text: The structure of the brain involved in taste sensation is
questions.explanation:
Composed of three short gyri and an additional ventral accessory gyrus, the anterior insula is home to the gustatory complex, which is integral to the representation of tastes, oral texture, and temperature.
Ref: Yiannakas A, Rosenblum K. The insula and taste learning. Frontiers in molecular neuroscience. 2017 Nov 3;10:335.

questions.question_text: Which of the following areas of the brain does not lack blood brain barrier?
questions.explanation: The anterior pituitary does not lack BBB. There are some areas of the brain that do not have a blood- brain barrier. These are so-called circum-ventricular organs e.g. subfornical organ, area postrema (chemo receptor trigger zone), median eminence and posterior pituitary. Here the capillaries are fenestrated like those in peripheral tissues

questions.question_text: The white matter tract connecting Wernicke's are and Broca's area is called
questions.explanation:
The arcuate fasciculus is a small bundle of nerve fibres in each cerebral hemisphere that curves round the back of the lateral sulcus and that in the (usually) left hemisphere connects Broca’s area with Wernicke’s area. Lesions to it often result in conduction aphasia.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which hypothalamic nucleus regulates prolactin secretion?
questions.explanation:
The arcuate nucleus is a small nucleus near the base of the hypothalamus containing the cell bodies that produce hypothalamic hormones. The prolactin-releasing factor is found in the arcuate nucleus. This activates the lactotrophic cells of the anterior pituitary. Dopamine, via the tuberoinfundibular dopaminergic system, regulates prolactin secretion through direct projection to the pituitary.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which of the following cells help in regulating potassium ion concentration in the extracellular space around neuronal cell body?
questions.explanation:
Several studies underline that reactive astrocytes alter homeostatic functions such as potassium ion uptake, ion buffering, calcium signalling, and excitatory neurotransmitter uptake.
Ref: Siracusa R et al. Astrocytes: role and functions in brain pathologies. Frontiers in pharmacology. 2019 Sep 27;10:1114.

questions.question_text: Acetylcholine is a substrate of which of the following substances?
questions.explanation:
Acetylcholine is formed in cholinergic neurons from two precursors: choline and acetyl coenzyme A (AcCoA). Choline is derived from dietary and intraneuronal sources, and AcCoA is made from glucose in the mitochondria of the neuron. These two substrates interact with the synthetic enzyme choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) to produce the neurotransmitter acetylcholine (ACh). ACh’s actions are terminated by one of two enzymes, acetylcholinesterase or butyrylcholinesterase. Both enzymes convert ACh into choline, which is then transported back into the presynaptic cholinergic neuron for resynthesis into ACh.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. p. 505.

questions.question_text: Which enzyme is required for the metabolism of the transmitter at the neuromuscular junction?
questions.explanation:
Acetylcholinesterase is an essential enzymatic component of the neuromuscular junction where it is responsible for terminating neurotransmission by the cholinergic motor neurons. The enzyme at the neuromuscular junction is contributed primarily by the skeletal muscle where is it produced at higher levels in the post-synaptic region of the fibres.
Ref: Rotundo RL. The NMJ as a model synapse: New perspectives on formation, synaptic transmission and maintenance:
Acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction. Neurosci Lett. 2020 Sep 14;735:135157. doi: 10.1016/j.neulet.2020.135157. Epub 2020 Jun 12. PMID: 32540360.

questions.question_text: The rate limiting enzyme in alcohol metabolism is
questions.explanation: The first step in the metabolism of alcohol is the oxidation of ethanol to acetaldehyde catalyzed by alcohol/dehydrogenase containing the coenzyme NAD+. The acetaldehyde is further oxidized to acetic acid and finally CO2 and water through the citric acid cycle. A number of metabolic effects from alcohol are directly linked to the production of an excess of both NADH and acetaldehyde

questions.question_text: Which among the following statements favour the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia?

options.text: Amphetamines release Dopamine into the synapse and cause positive schizophrenic symptoms
Disulfiram stimulates Dopamine metabolism and may exacerbate schizophrenia
Postal Emission Tomography (PET) shows decreased Dopamine receptor binding in drug naïve patients.
Both alpha and beta isomers of Flupenthixol are effective anti psychotic drugs

correct_answer.text: Amphetamines release Dopamine into the synapse and cause positive schizophrenic symptoms

correct_answers.text: Amphetamines release Dopamine into the synapse and cause positive schizophrenic symptoms

questions.explanation:
The simplest formulation of the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia posits that schizophrenia results from too much dopaminergic activity. The theory evolved from two observations. First, the efficacy and the potency of many antipsychotic drugs correlate with their ability to act as an antagonists of the dopamine type 2 receptor. Second, drugs that increase dopaminergic activity, notably cocaine and amphetamine, are psychotomimetic.
Only the alpha isomer of Flupentixol is a Dopamine antagonist and an effective anti psychotic drug. Phencyclidine causes both positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia but via antagonisms at the NMDA receptor. Disulfiram actually inhibits Dopamine metabolism and may exacerbate schizophrenia. PET studies show increased Dopamine receptor binding in drug-naive patients.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 361.

questions.question_text: Release of transmitters synthesized by neurons in the central nervous system is directly regulated by the concentration of which of the following electrolytes?
questions.explanation: Action potentials at the presynaptic axon terminals open up calcium channels, permitting calcium influx. This leads to movement of synaptic vesicles and subsequent release of stored neurotransmitters.

questions.question_text: The rate limiting step in the synthesis of serotonin is mediated by which of the following enzymes?
questions.explanation:
The rate-limiting step in serotonin synthesis is the hydroxylation of tryptophan by the enzyme tryptophan hydroxylase to form 5- hydroxytryptophan. Two isoforms of tryptophan hydroxylase exist – one isoform is found mainly in the periphery, whereas the second isoform is restricted to the CNS.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 957.

questions.question_text: In schizophrenia, dopamine deficiency is seen in which of the following brain regions?
questions.explanation:
The mesocortical dopamine (DA) pathway arises from cell bodies in the ventral tegmental area, projecting to areas of the prefrontal cortex. Branches of this pathway into the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex are hypothesised to regulate cognition and executive functions, whereas branches of this pathway into the ventromedial parts of the prefrontal cortex are hypothesised to regulate emotions and affect. The exact role of the mesocortical DA pathway in mediating symptoms of schizophrenia is still a matter of debate, but many researchers believe that cognitive and some negative symptoms of schizophrenia may be due to a deficit of DA activity in mesocortical projections to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex whereas affective and other negative symptoms of schizophrenia may be due to a deficit of DA activity in mesocortical projections to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. p. 95.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an agonist at the mu-opioid receptor?
questions.explanation:
Methadone is a full agonist at mu opioid receptors and has a long half-life (24 hours). Buprenorphine is a partial opioid agonist.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 478.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 636.

questions.question_text: A 75-year-old gentleman with memory problems, disinhibition and lack of insight. What microscopic findings will be expected in this case?
questions.explanation: This man is exhibiting symptoms of fronto-temporal dementia. The syndrome of FTD has been associated with two types of pathological change, which in individual cases cannot be predicted on clinical grounds. Tau positive inclusions account for the majority of cases, and most familial (but not sporadic) cases with tau pathology carry mutations in the microtubule-associated tau protein on chromosome 17. The other main pathological finding in FTD is so-called ubiquitin-only pathology with cytoplasmic and nuclear inclusions (i.e. negative for tau or alpha- synuclein), suggesting a link with Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

questions.question_text: A 37-year-old woman presents initially with optic neuritis and then with episodes of waxing and waning neurological deficits. The most likely pathological change in brain is
questions.explanation:
This patient has Multiple Sclerosis (MS), which is twice as common in women as in men. MS is an immune-mediated demyelinating disease. 85-90% of cases start with an episode of acute neurological symptoms (e.g., optic neuritis). Most patients follow a relapsing-remitting course.
Ref: Ron MA. The neuropsychiatry of multiple sclerosis. BJPsych Advances. 2018 May;24(3):178-87.

questions.question_text: A newborn child suffers from seizures and hydrocephalus. On examination, a midline facial anomaly and spasticity are evident. Further investigations reveal agenesis of corpus callosum. Which of the following underlying pathology is most likely?

options.text: Tissue loss secondary to obstetric trauma

questions.explanation:
Agenesis of the corpus callosum (ACC) has a varied background, ranging from maternal drinking, which is responsible for many defects in neural development, to prenatal infections, chromosomal errors, or gene mutations. The latter can present as isolated ACC or can be combined with other malformations that lead to syndromes (e.g., Coffin-Siris Syndrome). The most frequent causes of ACC are gene mutations that are related to pathways of axon guidance, ciliary development, cell adhesion, proliferation, differentiation, and migration.
Ref: Hofman J et al. Corpus callosum agenesis: an insight into the etiology and spectrum of symptoms. Brain Sciences. 2020 Sep;10(9):625. http://www.ninds.nih.gov/disorders/neuronal_migration/neuronal_migration.htm

questions.question_text: In which of the following conditions brain biopsy can show lesions with intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies?
questions.explanation:
Pathological features of Lewy body dementia include eosinophilic A-synuclein neuronal inclusions (Lewy bodies), with neuronal loss in brainstem nuclei (especially basal ganglia) and paralimbic and neocortical structures.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 162.

questions.question_text: Which of the following EEG wavelets have low amplitude and high frequency?
questions.explanation:
Beta waves have high (more than 13Hz) frequency but low amplitude.
Ref: Boutros NN, Galderisi S, Pogarell O, Riggio S. Standard electroencephalography in clinical psychiatry: A practical handbook. 2011.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a gut hormone released from small intestine in response to fats and proteins and serves to regulate food intake?
questions.explanation:
Cholecystokinin is a peptide hormone released by the small intestine that helps to signal satiety during food consumption.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 479.

questions.question_text: The suprachiasmatic nucleus plays an important role in which of the following functions?
questions.explanation:
The key neurobiological regulator of the circadian sleep system is the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus.
Ref: Smith PC, Mong JA. Neuroendocrine control of sleep. Neuroendocrine Regulation of Behavior. 2019:353-78.

questions.question_text: Miss. X suffers from eating disorder characterized by binge eating, body image disturbances and measures taken to reduce weight . This condition is associated with reduced levels of
questions.explanation:
Changes in leptin and ghrelin occur in patients with anorexia or bulimia nervosa and have been suggested to represent not only homeostatic adaptations to an altered energy balance but to contribute also to the acquisition and/or maintenance of persistent starvation, binge eating, and physical hyperactivity, which are potentially rewarding for eating disordered patients.
Ref: Monteleone AM et al. Neuroendocrinology and brain imaging of reward in eating disorders: a possible key to the treatment of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa. Progress in neuro-psychopharmacology and biological psychiatry. 2018 Jan 3;80:132-42.

questions.question_text: REM sleep behaviour disorder is associated with
questions.explanation:
REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD) is a parasomnia manifested by recurrent dream enactment behaviour associated with an absence of normal REM sleep atonia. It occurs in 76% of cases of dementia with Lewy bodies. It is also associated with other disorders such as Parkinson's disease, multi-system atrophy and Guillain Barre syndrome. RBD may be seen in the prodrome of DLB and Parkinson's disease.
Ref: McKeith IG et al. Diagnosis and management of dementia with Lewy bodies: Fourth consensus report of the DLB Consortium. Neurology. 2017 Jul 4;89(1):88-100.

questions.question_text: Phenothiazines that are associated with pigment deposits in anterior lens capsule include
questions.explanation:
High-dose chlorpromazine can result in abnormal pigmentation of the eyelids, cornea, and lens. However, this is not associated with visual disturbance and resolves on cessation of treatment. Thioridazine (now withdrawn) was also associated with pigmentary retinopathy. Corneal oedema can also (rarely) occur with chlorpromazine, leading to loss of vision if treatment is not withdrawn.
Ref: Taylor DM, Gaughran F, Pillinger T. The Maudsley Practice Guidelines for Physical Health Conditions in Psychiatry. 2021. p. 519.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a risk factor for neuroleptic-induced akathisia?
questions.explanation: Female gender and older age are risk factors for akathisia.

questions.question_text: In the setting of tardive dyskinesia, switching or withdrawing antipsychotic medication is not always effective or advisable. Which of the following has been shown to be an effective add-on agent for the treatment of tardive dyskinesia?
questions.explanation:
The use of pyridoxine (vitamin B6) as an add-on agent for the treatment of tardive dyskinesia is supported by Cochrane and meta-analysis data. It can be dosed up to 400mg/day.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 118.

questions.question_text: The most well-established risk factor in terms of developing tardive dyskinesia when using antipsychotics is
questions.explanation:
The most consistent factor predisposing to the development of tardive dyskinesia is age - the older the patient, the greater the risk. There is up to 6-fold greater incidence in those first exposed to antipsychotics in middle to late life. Other risk factors include antipsychotic potency, number of antipsychotic-free intervals, previous (early) extrapyramidal symptoms, affective disorders, organicity (leucotomy, structural brain changes, negative (deficit) symptoms), and genetics.
Ref: Owens DC. Tardive dyskinesia update: the syndrome. BJPsych Advances. 2019 Jan;25(1):57-69.

questions.question_text: Fetal Ebstein anomaly is associated with which of the following psychotropic medications?
questions.explanation:
Much attention has been focused on the rare but severe cardiac anomaly of the Ebstein type. There may be an increased risk of Ebstein anomaly (prevalence in the general population of 1:20 000) if lithium taken during 1st trimester (maximum risk 2-6 weeks after conception), though the size of risk uncertain. More recent data suggest the magnitude of effect is much smaller than previously estimated. Recent data have shown an association with maternal mental health problems generally rather than specifically with lithium.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 690.
McAllister-Williams RH et al. British Association for Psychopharmacology consensus guidance on the use of psychotropic medication preconception, in pregnancy and postpartum 2017. Journal of Psychopharmacology. 2017 May;31(5):519-52.

questions.question_text: A woman comes into Emergency Department with vomitting, diarrhoea and severe tremors with weight loss on a hot afternoon. She is taking some unknown psychotropic medication for a long time. She is recently started on 'water tablets' for swelling in her legs. Which of the following is a likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.explanation:
The story here is suggestive of lithium overdose or toxicity. Diuretics can reduce the renal clearance of lithium, the magnitude of this effect being greater with thiazide than loop diuretics. Lithium levels usually rise within 10 days of a thiazide diuretic (e.g. bendroflumethiazide, chlortalidone, inadapamide, xipamide) being prescribed. Although there are case reports of lithium toxicity induced by loop diuretics, many patients receive loop diuretics (e.g. furosemide) together with lithium without apparent problems.
Hot weather with dehydration is another important risk factor for precipitating lithium toxicity. The person can present with vomiting, diarrhoea and severe tremors.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 253.

questions.question_text: The factors that increase the risk of agranulocytosis in patients treated with clozapine include all of the following except
questions.explanation:
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 236.
Mijovic A, MacCabe JH. Clozapine-induced agranulocytosis. Annals of Hematology. 2020 Aug 20:1-6.
Silva E et al. Clozapine rechallenge and initiation despite neutropenia-a practical, step-by-step guide. BMC psychiatry. 2020 Dec;20:1-9.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is the least likely feature associated with Neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Myoclonus is a feature that could be seen in serotonin syndrome and not in NMS.
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS):
Differentiating NMS from serotonin syndrome:
Ref: Volpi-Abadie J et al. Serotonin syndrome. Ochsner Journal. 2013 Dec 21;13(4):533-40.
Taylor DM, Gaughran F, Pillinger T. The Maudsley Practice Guidelines for Physical Health Conditions in Psychiatry. 2021.

questions.question_text: A common side effect of sildenafil is
questions.explanation:
Common side effects of phosphodiesterase inhibitors (such as sildenafil and tadalafil) are mild headaches, dizziness, and nasal congestion.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 176.

questions.question_text: Tom recently underwent an alcohol detoxification programme. Upon achieving abstinence, he was keen on anti-craving treatment and has been started on acamprosate. Which one among the following is a common side effect of acamprosate?
questions.explanation:
Acamprosate is relatively well tolerated; adverse effects include diarrhoea, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and pruritus.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 463.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following has a high hepatotoxic potential?
questions.explanation:
Rare cases of sometimes fatal hepatotoxicity led the original manufacturer to discontinue the production of branded nefazodone in 2004. Generic nefazodone remains available in the United States.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 638.

questions.question_text: Low serum iron is associated with which of the following side effects related to neuroleptic medication treatment?
questions.explanation:
A lesser-known risk factor for neuroleptic malignant syndrome is low serum iron.
Ref: Patil BS et al. Low serum iron as a possible risk factor for neuroleptic malignant syndrome. International Journal of Applied and Basic Medical Research. 2014 Jul;4(2):117.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old gentleman with depression has been started on Tranylcypromine. Which drug is safe to be taken?
questions.explanation:
Tranylcypromine is a MAOI Inhibitor. Serotonin toxicity, often referred to as serotonin syndrome, is an iatrogenic drug-induced toxidrome associated with raised intra-synaptic concentrations of serotonin (5-HT) in the CNS. Dangerous toxic reactions, including death, have been shown to result after the administration of meperidine (pethidine – an opioid analgesic drug used in anaesthesia) to patients taking an MAOI such as phenelzine or tranylcypromine. Other opioids to avoid when taking tranylcypromine include tramadol and methadone. Over-the- counter medications to avoid include cold and cough preparations, including those containing dextromethorphan, decongestants (e.g. phenylephrine, pseudoephedrine), hay fever medication, sinus medications, asthma inhalant medications, weight reducing preparations, and ‘pep’ pills.
Ref: Baldo BA, Rose MA. The anaesthetist, opioid analgesic drugs, and serotonin toxicity: a mechanistic and clinical review. British journal of anaesthesia. 2020 Jan 1;124(1):44-62.
Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber’s Guide, 7th Edition. 2021. p. 789.

questions.question_text: According to CATIE study, which drug had the lowest drop out rate when treating schizophrenia?
questions.explanation:
CATIE stands for Clinical Antipsychotic Trials of Intervention Effectiveness. The study design was double-blind pragmatic RCT. 1493 patients with chronic schizophrenia were included and randomised to one of the following: Olanzapine, Quetiapine, Risperidone, Ziprasidone (added later in the trial), Perphenazine. The primary outcome was a 'real-world' measure - discontinuation for any reason (irrespective of whether patient-initiated or physician-initiated). Irrespective of the prescribed drug - 74% discontinued treatment in 18 months (surprisingly high despite naturalistic design). Median time to discontinue was 4.6 months. Olanzapine had lowest discontinuation rate (still 64%) - but highest side effect burden. 64% discontinued olanzapine; 75%, perphenazine; 82%, quetiapine; 74%, risperidone; and 79%, ziprasidone.
Ref: Swartz MS et al. Special section on implications of CATIE: what CATIE found: results from the schizophrenia trial. Psychiatric services. 2008 May;59(5):500-6.

questions.question_text: Which of the following adverse effect of clozapine is mediated via alpha adrenoceptor blockade?
questions.explanation:
Clozapine’s blockade of alpha-1 adrenergic receptors can cause dizziness, hypotension, and syncope.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber’s Guide, 7th Edition. 2021. p. 193.

questions.question_text: Mr Y is a 45-year-old gentleman with history of schizophrenia. He suffers from akathisia due to taking risperidone and also has some depressive symptoms. The drug of choice in his case would be
questions.explanation:
There is limited evidence for efficacy for any pharmacological treatment for akathisia. Options include switching to an antipsychotic with a lower liability for the condition, or adding a beta-adrenergic blocker, a 5-HT2A antagonist (such as mirtazapine or mianserin), or an anticholinergic agent.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 111.

questions.question_text: Buprenorphine acts on which receptor?
questions.explanation:
Buprenorphine is a partial agonist at mu-opioid receptors.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 478.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old woman with a past history of psychotic depression is having a relapse but is managed by the Crisis and Home Treatment team in the community. She is currently on lofepramine 180 mg and risperidone 2 mg at bedtime. After a week, she reports to the community worker who visited her at home that her nipples are leaking. She is very concerned and denies she could be pregnant. Which class of medications is most commonly known to cause this problem?
questions.explanation:
When D2 antagonists (neuroleptics) are administered, D2 receptors in the tuberoinfundibular dopamine pathway are blocked. This causes plasma prolactin concentrations to rise, a condition called hyperprolactinaemia. This can be associated with galactorrhea (i.e. breast secretions), sexual dysfunction, gynaecomastia (enlargement of the breasts) in men, and amenorrhea (i.e. irregular or lack of menstrual periods) in women.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. pp. 164-165.

questions.question_text: A 50 year old man is treated for erectile dysfunction using sildenafil as and when required. Availability of which of the following vasodilatory substances is increased by sildenafil?
questions.explanation:
The discovery in the late 1980s of nitric oxide (NO) as the endothelium-derived relaxing factor was key to understanding the NO-soluble GC (sGC)-cGMP pathway. NO mediates its biological effects by activating sGC and increasing cGMP synthesis which, in turn, activates certain proteins resulting in different actions. cGMP actions are terminated by phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5). The synthesis of sildenafil, a PGE-5 inhibitor, and the (serendipity) discovery of its effects on penile erection provided a breakthrough in the treatment of erectile dysfunction and opened new fields of clinical application for this class of drug.
Ref: Andersson KE. PDE5 inhibitors–pharmacology and clinical applications 20 years after sildenafil discovery. British journal of pharmacology. 2018 Jul;175(13):2554-65.

questions.question_text: Riluzole prevents the release of which neurotransmitter?
questions.explanation:
Riluzole was developed to slow the progression of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS, or Lou Gehrig disease). Theoretically, riluzole binds to voltage-sensitive sodium channels and prevents glutamate release, in an action similar to that proposed for lamotrigine. The idea is that diminishing glutamate release would prevent the postulated excitotoxicity that may be causing the death of motor neurons in ALS.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. pp. 352-353.

questions.question_text: The mechanism of action of Memantine is
questions.explanation:
The mechanism of memantine involves blockade of N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA) glutamate receptors. Unlike ketamine which is a high- affinity noncompetitive blocker, memantine is a non-competitive blocker with low affinity and binds only to actively open NMDA channels. Its receptor dissociation rate is relatively fast, and so it does not accumulate and interfere with normal NMDA activity.
Characteristics of cognitive enhancers:
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 605-606.

questions.question_text: What is the mechanism of action of atomoxetine when used in the treatment of ADHD?
questions.explanation:
Atomoxetine is a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (NRI). Blocking norepinephrine transporters (NETs) in the prefrontal cortex increases both dopamine and norepinephrine (NE) in the prefrontal cortex and is why NET inhibitors are thought to work in ADHD. However, since there are few NE neurons and NETs in nucleus accumbens, inhibiting NET does not lead to an increase in either NE or DA there and is why NET inhibitors are thought not to have reinforcing, abuse, or addiction potential.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. p. 480.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following properties is not a significant effect of Trazodone?
questions.explanation:
Trazodone blocks the serotonin transporter at antidepressant doses. It also has serotonin 2A and 2C, H1 histamine, and alpha-1-adrenergic antagonist properties, which can make it very sedating. At low doses, trazodone does not adequately block serotonin reuptake but retains its other properties.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. p. 535.

questions.question_text: A patient who needs a prescription for a new antidepressant is almost certain that he will miss one or two tablets during his treatment due to the nature of his job. What is the most suitable choice of medications?
questions.explanation:
Due to its longer half-life, missing fluoxetine for a day or two will not usually cause acute withdrawal symptoms. Fluoxetine has a long half- life (2-3 days) and its active metabolite (norfluoxetine) an even longer half-life (2 weeks). Fluoxetine has a long half-life when compared with other SSRIs.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. p. 293.
Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 562, 742.

questions.question_text: The effect of which of the following groups of drugs is least influenced by their pharmacokinetics?
questions.explanation:
MAOIs such as phenelzine, tranylcypromine, and isocarboxazid are readily absorbed after oral administration and reach peak plasma concentrations with in 2 hours. Whereas their plasma half-lives are in the range of 2-3 hours, their tissue half-lives are considerably longer. They are irreversible enzyme inhibitors, and thus enzyme activity returns only after new enzyme is synthesised about 2-3 weeks later. Thus, the activity of these drugs depends less on pharmacokinetics and more on the synthesis of new MAO to restore normal enzyme activity.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 645.
Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. p. 337.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a cardinal feature of depression?
questions.explanation:
The two central clinical features of depressive illness are: (1) pervasively depressed and unreactive mood; and 2) anhedonia – the loss of pleasure in previously pleasurable activities.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 63.

questions.question_text: Which of the following clinical features suggests a diagnosis of mania rather than hypomania?
questions.explanation:
By definition (in both DSM-5 and ICD-11), hypomania is not severe enough to interfere with social or occupational functioning, require admission to hospital, or include psychotic features (delusions or hallucinations).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 322.

questions.question_text: Mrs Pinto lost her husband 9 months ago. She had continued attending her bingo sessions and cathedral groups since his death, but recently she has had pervasive guilt and suicidal thoughts. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Characteristics outside the normal range of grief - that may be indicative of depression – include preoccupation with feelings of worthlessness, thoughts of death, excessive guilt, marked slowing of thoughts and movements, a prolonged period of not being able to function normally, and hallucinatory experiences (other than the image or voice of the deceased).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 400.

questions.question_text: A 37-year-old woman was admitted to the medical ward with history of sudden onset aphonia. Physical examination and investigations were normal. Her boyfriend has recently invited his mother to stay with them permanently, as his mother is feeling lonely and isolated. What is the most likely diagnosis according to ICD-11 criteria?
questions.explanation:
Dissociative neurological symptom disorder, with speech disturbance is characterised by symptoms such as difficulty with speaking (dysphonia), loss of the ability to speak (aphonia), or difficult or unclear articulation of speech (dysarthria) that are not consistent with a recognised disease of the nervous system, a neurodevelopmental or neurocognitive disorder, other mental, behavioural, or neurodevelopmental disorder, or other medical condition and do not occur exclusively during another dissociative disorder.
Ref: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed; ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

questions.question_text: A soldier is referred with symptoms of PTSD following return from Iraq. Which of the following feature is not consistent with the diagnosis of PTSD?

options.text: He is not able to enjoy watching television
He is not able to share his war experience with his close friends
He sleeps in his day time clothes
He is keen to go to Iraq again
He has sustained only mild injuries physically

correct_answer.text: He is keen to go to Iraq again

correct_answers.text: He is keen to go to Iraq again

questions.explanation:
Post-traumatic stress disorder is characterised by: (1) Re-experiencing the traumatic event(s) in the present in the form of vivid intrusive memories, flashbacks, or nightmares; (2) Avoidance of thoughts and memories of the event(s), or avoidance of activities, situations, or people reminiscent of the event(s); (3) Persistent perceptions of heightened current threat, for example as indicated by hypervigilance or an enhanced startle reaction to stimuli such as unexpected noises.
Avoidance is a part of PTSD - wanting to go back to Iraq is not consistent with this.
Ref: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed; ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

questions.question_text: Mrs Broadbent was diagnosed with compensation neurosis a few decades ago. Which of the following is true regarding this?

options.text: Severe difficulties with sleep are noted
Most patients do not return to work even after settlement
Higher the severity of injury, greater the symptoms of compensation neurosis
Improvements tend to occur after financial settlement

correct_answer.text: Most patients do not return to work even after settlement

correct_answers.text: Most patients do not return to work even after settlement

questions.explanation:
Compensation neurosis is not an ICD diagnosis; its validity is questionable. Patients show scant improvement even after financial settlement. A follow-up study of 760 litigants found that, of the 264 subjects who were not working at the time of conclusion of litigation and who could be traced, 198 (75%) were not working after an average of 23 months following the finalization of their cases. (Mendelson, 1995.
Compensation neurosis revisited. Journal of Psychosomatic Research, 39, pp. 695-706)

questions.question_text: An elderly man presents with fluctuation in consciousness and visual hallucinations. His wife reports that he is not able to turn in his bed properly. You suspect
questions.explanation:
Not able to turn in bed indicates axial rigidity that may be related to Parkinsonism. His presentation suggests Lewy body dementia.
Ref: Tampi RR et al. Psychotic disorders in late life: a narrative review. Therapeutic advances in psychopharmacology. 2019 Oct;9:1-13.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is consistent with a diagnosis of bipolar affective disorder, currently hypomanic episode?
questions.explanation:
As defined in ICD-11, a hypomanic episode is a persistent mood state lasting at least several days characterised by mild elevation of mood or increased irritability and increased activity of a subjective experience of increased energy, accompanied by other characteristic symptoms such as rapid speech, rapid or racing thoughts, increased self-esteem, an increase in sexual drive or sociability, decreased need for sleep, distractibility, or impulsive or reckless behaviour. The symptoms are not severe enough to cause marked impairment in occupational functioning or in usual activities or relationships with other, does not necessitate hospitalisation, and there are no accompanying delusions or hallucinations.
Ref: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed; ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

questions.question_text: Which of the following features is included in ICD-11 diagnosis for generalised anxiety disorder?
questions.explanation:
As defined in ICD-11, generalised anxiety disorder is characterised by marked symptoms of anxiety that persist for at least several months, for more days than not, manifested by either general apprehension (i.e. ‘free-floating anxiety’) or excessive worry focused on multiple everyday events, most often concerning family, health, finances, and school or work, together with additional symptoms of muscular tension or motor restlessness, sympathetic autonomic over-activity, subjective experience of nervousness, difficulty maintaining concentration, irritability, or sleep disturbance.
Ref: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed; ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

questions.question_text: A 33-year-old lady presents with excessive day time sleepiness and auditory hallucinations when waking from sleep. She also recalls episodes of feeling 'pinned down' to her bed even after waking up. The likely diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
Classic symptoms of narcolepsy include: (1) Excessive daytime sleepiness; (2) Cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone during wakefulness that is evoked by strong, mainly positive, emotions); (3) Sleep paralysis (sometimes up to 10 minutes long); (4) Hypnagogic hallucinations (vivid hallucinations on falling asleep) or hypnopompic hallucinations (hallucinations when the individual is waking up).
The symptoms described here include excessive daytime sleepiness, hypnopompic hallucinations, and sleep paralysis.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 450.
Kornum BR et al. Narcolepsy. Nature reviews Disease primers. 2017 Feb 9;3(1):1-9.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not a negative symptom of schizophrenia?
questions.explanation:
Negative symptoms of schizophrenia include: (1) Flattened affect (limited affective responsiveness); (2) Alogia (poverty of speech); (3)
Anhedonia (inability to experience pleasure); (4) Social withdrawal (lack of desire to form relationships); (5) Avolition (lack of motivation); (6) Lethargy; (7) Attentional impairment.
Ref: Barnes TR et al. Evidence-based guidelines for the pharmacological treatment of schizophrenia: Updated recommendations from the British Association for Psychopharmacology. Journal of Psychopharmacology. 2020 Jan;34(1):3-78.

questions.question_text: Simultaneous presence of contrasting attitudes towards a person, an action or an idea is called
questions.explanation:
Ambivalence is the coexistence of two opposing impulses toward the same thing in the same person at the same time.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1135.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following terms describes fantasy thinking?
questions.explanation:
There are three types of thinking: (1) Undirected fantasy thinking (also termed autistic or dereistic thinking) which is quite common, but certain individuals when faced with repeated disappointments or adverse life circumstances may engage in excessive undirected fantasy thinking; (2) Imaginative thinking, which does not go beyond the rational and the possible; (3) Rational thinking or conceptual thinking, which attempts to solve a problem.
Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 43.

questions.question_text: A man with epilepsy answers a question correctly, but only after including multiple unnecessary and trivial details. This form of speech is called
questions.explanation:
Circumstantiality occurs when thinking proceeds slowly with many unnecessary and trivial details, but finally the point is reached. The goal of thinking is never completely lost and thinking proceeds towards it by an intricate and convoluted path. Historically, this has been regarded as a feature of the constellation of personality traits occasionally associated with epilepsy. Circumstantiality, however, can also occur in the context of intellectual disability and in individuals with obsessional personality traits, as well as schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder.
Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 45.

questions.question_text: The most common form of synesthesia is
questions.explanation:
Synaesthesia is the experience of a stimulus in one sense modality producing a sensory experience in another (e.g. tasting sounds or hearing colours). Over 60 types of synaesthetic phenomena have been described. The apparently most common form (with a 64.4% prevalence among synaesthetes) is grapheme-colour synaesthesia, in which achromatic letters or digits automatically trigger an idiosyncratic colour perceptual experience (e.g., the number ‘4’ induces blue colour percepts).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 118.
Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 36.
Safran AB, Sanda N. Color synesthesia. Insight into perception, emotion, and consciousness. Current opinion in neurology. 2015 Feb;28(1):36.

questions.question_text: Mr. Smith experiences repetitive intrusive images of corpses of his family members in coffins. He had to imagine the same people alive to reduce the anxiety associated with the experience. This compensatory attempt is best described as
questions.explanation:
In OCD, obsessions are repetitive unwanted thoughts, images, or urges. Compulsions are repetitive behaviours or thoughts that are often, but not always, performed to address anxiety associated with obsessions. The drive to perform a compulsion is recognised by the patient as their own (i.e. there is not sense of ‘possession’ or passivity), but it is associated with a subjective sense of need to perform it, often in order to avoid the occurrence of an adverse event. The patient may resist carrying out the compulsion for a time, at the expense of mounting anxiety.
Two types of recurrent images may be described in OCD. Obsessive image refers to recurrent images that are recognised as irrelevant, senseless appearing in one's own mind but with no willful control. Sometimes patients may voluntarily produce images that are counter- intuitive in order to negate the feared effects of such obsessive images - these are called as compulsive images.
Ref: Hirschtritt ME, Bloch MH, Mathews CA. Obsessive-compulsive disorder: advances in diagnosis and treatment. Jama. 2017 Apr 4;317(13):1358-67.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 104.

questions.question_text: On a nice sunny day you are driving along a country road where you have never been before. You suddenly have a sense of familiarity for the place. This is known as:
questions.explanation:
Déjà vu is a sense that events being experienced for the first time have been experienced before. Jamais vu is the sensation that events or situations are unfamiliar, although they have been experienced before. Both déjà vu and jamais vu can be everyday experiences, but also non-specific symptoms of a number of disorders, including temporal lobe epilepsy, schizophrenia, and anxiety disorders.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 105, 113.

questions.question_text: A 49-year-old lady repeatedly presents to police asking them to arrest her for a murder despite never having committed this crime. This condition is known as:
questions.explanation:
A delusion of guilt is a delusional belief that one has committed a crime or other reprehensible act. It can be a feature of psychotic depressive illness.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 107.

questions.question_text: "Today I took a train from Derby to Matlock with Jeff, my dog. I carried my knife and pepper spray as we walk through the town, as I am convinced someone will abduct and mutilate me and kill Jeff". This can be described as a
questions.explanation:
A persecutory delusion is a delusional belief that one’s life is being interfered with in a harmful way. Some patients believe that they or their loved one are about to be killed, or are being tortured.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 115.
Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 50.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old woman in a psychiatric inpatient unit complains that someone is injecting blood into her body on a regular basis. On further questioning she points to a black mole in her hand as an explanation for her belief. This is best termed as
questions.explanation:
A delusional elaboration is a secondary delusion which arises in a manner which is understandable as the patient attempting to find explanations for primary psychopathological processes (e.g. a patient with persistent auditory hallucinations developing a belief that a transmitter has been placed in their ear).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 106.

questions.question_text: Which of the following attachment behaviour pattern has been commonly reported in children subjected to abuse?
questions.explanation:
Mary Ainsworth devised the Strange Situation procedure with 12- to 18-month infants, which categorised infant-parent relationships into three distinct groups: secure, insecure avoidant, and insecure ambivalent. The procedure involves separations and reunions with caregivers and observes response. A fourth category, disorganised, was added by Mary Main in 1986. Bizarre, confused, or contradictory behaviour is characteristic of disorganised attachment behaviour. It is often associated with maltreatment/abuse and/or parental trauma.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 658-659.

questions.question_text: Fears that show no particular age trend include:
questions.explanation:
Fears that show no particular age trend include fear of snakes or storms. While babies and very young children do not usually fear snakes, they are unusually skilled at detecting them and show a predisposition to learn to fear snakes if they have bad experiences or even if they are exposed to negative portrayals of them in the media.
Souchet J, Aubret F. Revisiting the fear of snakes in children: the role of aposematic signalling. Scientific reports. 2016 Nov 25;6(1):1-7.

questions.question_text: Deductive reasoning is achieved in which stage of Piaget's cognitive development theory?
questions.explanation:
According to Piaget, the stage of formal operations lasts from about 11 years of age through the end of adolescence. The stage is so named because young persons’ thinking operates in a formal, highly logical, systematic, and symbolic manner. It is characterised by the ability to think abstractly, to reason deductively, and to define concepts, and also by the emergence of skills for dealing with permutations and combinations. Adolescents attempt to deal with all possible relations and hypotheses to explain data and events during this stage. Hypotheticodeductive thinking, the highest organisation of cognition, enables people to make a hypothesis or proposition and to test it against reality. Deductive reasoning moves from the general to the particular and is more complicated process than inductive reasoning, which moves from the particular to the general.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1009.
Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: An 8-year-old boy is most likely to fall under which stage of Erikson's psychosocial development?
questions.explanation:
Erik Erikson created an original and highly influential theory of psychological development and crisis occurring in periods that extended across the entire life cycle. Stage 4 takes place from about 5 years to about 13 years. Its focus is industry versus inferiority. The child develops industry by learning new skills and takes pride in the things made. A child unprepared for this stage of psychosocial development, either through an insufficient resolution of previous stages or by current interference, may develop a sense of inferiority and inadequacy.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 1071-1074.

questions.question_text: In Ainsworth's strange situation experiment, a child showed no signs of distress at leaving the mother and ignored her on return. Which type of attachment behaviour is this?
questions.explanation:
Mary Ainsworth devised the Strange Situation procedure with 12- to 18-month infants, which categorised infant-parent relationships. The procedure involves separations and reunions with caregivers and observes response. In insecure-avoidant attachment, the child seems unconcerned at separation or reunion. It is associated with unresponsive parenting.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 658-659.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is associated with classifying personality according to body build?
questions.explanation:
Ernst Kretschmer theorised that there are four basic body types, each associated with its own distinctive pattern of personality characteristics: (1) Aesthetic: slender, long-limbed; (2) Athletic: muscular, well-built; (3) Dysplastic: misshapen, ugly; (4) Pyknic: short, squat, rounded.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which type of learning behaviour occurs without apparent reward or reinforcement?
questions.explanation:
Latent learning is animal learning that occurs without any apparent reinforcement or reward, as when a rat explores a maze and is later shown to have learned to find its way around it. In human learning, the phenomenon is called incidental learning.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements about memory loss following ECT is incorrect?

options.text: Memory impairment is more pronounced with unilateral ECT
The period closest to receiving ECT is the least well-remembered in patients with ECT-related memory issues
A third of patients report persistent memory loss in some surveys
There may be both anterograde and retrograde amnesia
Most studies did not measure autobiographical memory over the long term

correct_answer.text: Memory impairment is more pronounced with unilateral ECT

correct_answers.text: Memory impairment is more pronounced with unilateral ECT

questions.explanation:
Memory loss following ECT is usually temporary, and both anterograde and retrograde amnesia are reported. A third of patients may report persistent memory loss following ECT (Rose et al., 2003). Research has focused on retrograde amnesia because of highly publicised claims that ECT causes more enduring deficits in past memories (especially autobiographical) than new memories. Research shows that the period closest to receiving ECT is least well-remembered and can be permanently lost. Autobiographical loss does occur and is related to how ECT is administered. Recommendations to minimise memory loss include: use of right unilateral ECT; brief pulse, rather than sine wave, ECT; dose titration; and limited number and frequency of ECT sessions.
Ref: Rose D, Wykes T, Leese M, et al. Patients’ perspectives on electroconvulsive therapy: systematic review. BMJ 2003;326:1363.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 308.

questions.question_text: Which of the following instruments assess personality as a construct spread over ten clinical scales?
questions.explanation:
The Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI) is a self-report questionnaire consisting of 567 questions covering eight areas of psychopathology and two areas of personality type. The scales are: Hypochondriasis, Depression, Hysteria, Psychopathic deviate, Masculinity-femininity, Paranoia, Psychasthenia, Schizophrenia, Hypomania, and Social introversion. There are also four additional validity (test-taking attitude) scales.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 96.
Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following is an objective personality test?
questions.explanation:
The Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI) is a self-report questionnaire consisting of 567 questions covering eight areas of psychopathology and two areas of personality type. The scales are: Hypochondriasis, Depression, Hysteria, Psychopathic deviate, Masculinity-femininity, Paranoia, Psychasthenia, Schizophrenia, Hypomania, and Social introversion. There are also four additional validity (test-taking attitude) scales.
Projective (non-objective) tests of personality include the Rorschach test (10 cards), Thematic Apperception Test (TAT-with pictures of persons and scenes), Sentence Completion Test, Holtzman Inkblot Technique (TIT), Figure drawing (typically human forms but can involve houses or other forms e.g. Draw-a-Person-Test or DAPT) and Make-a-Picture Story (MAPS).
Cattell 16 PF scale is an objective personality test devised from a nonclinical population. It includes a lie scale, frequency and correction scales.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 96 Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 59.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following is a feature of attentional processing according to Shiffrin and Schneider's divided attention theory?
questions.explanation: According to Shiffrin and Schneider's divided attention theory (1977), automatic processing is unconscious, not limited, automatic through extensive training, and once learnt are resistant to change. But Attentional (controlled) processing is consciously directed, needs focussed attention and more mental effort and also has limited capacity.

questions.question_text: Which of the following offers a psychological explanation regarding the aetiology of OCD?
questions.explanation:
Psychologically, obsessions are conditioned (neutral) stimuli, associated with an anxiety-provoking event. Compulsions are learnt and negatively reinforced, as they are a form of anxiety-reducing avoidance.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 385.

questions.question_text: Star chart is based on the principles of
questions.explanation:
Behaviour modification is based on operant conditioning. Forms of behavioural modification include the use of secondary reinforcement, such as ‘token economy’, in which socially desirable/acceptable behaviours are rewarded with tokens that can be exchanged for other material items or privileges, or ‘star charts’ where children’s good behaviour is rewarded when a certain level is achieved.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 908.

questions.question_text: Which part of the brain is involved in mediating performances in short term memory?

options.text: Entorhinal cortex of the medial temporal lobe

questions.explanation: Brain imaging and neuropsychological studies provide strong evidence that a.The brain areas mediating performances in STM are principally the pre-frontal lobes b.The phonological STM system is mediated by the left hemisphere regions of Broca's' area and prefrontal cortex. c.The visuospatial STM system is mediated by the parietal and prefrontal areas of the right hemisphere. d.The brain areas responsible for LTM includes the regions of the limbic system especially the hippocampus and the Entorhinal cortex of the medial temporal lobe.

questions.question_text: A candidate who has appeared for a mock exam before the actual exam does better than a candidate who has not. This is called
questions.explanation: Practice effects occur when a participant in an experiment performs a task after having performed the same task earlier. Subjects can either have a positive (subjects become better at performing the task) or negative (subjects become worse at performing the task) effect. Repeated measures designs are almost always affected by practice effects.

questions.question_text: The most common effect of cognitive dissonance is
questions.explanation:
Cognitive dissonance is a motivating state of tension or distress that tends to generate three types of dissonance-reducing behaviour: changing one of the cognitions, decreasing the perceived importance of the dissonant cognitions, and/or adding further (justifying) cognitions (the easiest and commonest method of dissonance reduction).
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: A Malaysian man shows sudden excitement with marked violence after a period of withdrawal. He returns to premorbid state after a violent incident. This is called as
questions.explanation:
Amok is a dissociative episode characterised by a period of depression followed by an outburst of violent, aggressive, or homicidal behaviour. Episodes tend to be caused by a perceived insult and are often accompanied by persecutory ideas, automation, amnesia, and exhaustion. Patients return to premorbid states following the episode. Amok seems to be prevalent only among males. The term originated in Malaysia.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1053.

questions.question_text: The following is true about the prima facie (main) principles of medical ethics:

options.text: Virtue theory: principle based on the characteristics of moral agents
Autonomy: Respecting patient's views despite disagreement
Utilitarianism: principle based on the greatest benefit for the greater number of people
Deontology: principle based on the act as stemming from duties irrespective of the moral agent characteristics
Teleology: principle based on consequences of the act

correct_answer.text: Autonomy: Respecting patient's views despite disagreement

correct_answers.text: Autonomy: Respecting patient's views despite disagreement

questions.explanation:
The four principles of Beauchamp and Childress – autonomy, non-maleficence, beneficence, and justice – have been extremely influential in the field of medical ethics. Autonomy requires that a person act intentionally after being given sufficient information and time to understand the benefits, risks, and costs of all options.
Note that even though the pairs are correct with respect to the explanations attached, except autonomy the other ethical principles stated here belong to 'higher-order' values.
Ref: Page K. The four principles: Can they be measured and do they predict ethical decision making?. BMC medical ethics. 2012 Dec;13(1):1-8. Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 829.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is most associated with an increased risk of developing schizophrenia?

options.text: Being frequently placed in a 'double-bind situation' as a child
Being born in an urban area
Experiencing high expressed emotion in the family home

correct_answer.text: Being born in an urban area

correct_answers.text: Being born in an urban area

questions.explanation:
Urbanisation at birth has been associated with an increased risk of schizophrenia.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 191.

questions.question_text: When a psychiatric patient is unwell, family members who advocate for admission to a mental hospital are unlikely to provide a realistic picture of what the patient will experience. After hospitalisation, the patient may feel 'conned' by them. What was the term used by Goffman to describe this?
questions.explanation:
Erving Goffman was a Canadian-born US sociologist whose writing provides insights into the mental hospital environment, particularly as experienced by patients. He suggested that family who advocate for admission to a mental hospital are unlikely to provide a realistic picture of what the patient will experience. The patient will be told that they will get required medical treatment and a rest, and then be released. In some cases, these advocates of admission to a mental hospital may be concealing what they know, but more likely they will be telling what they believe to be the truth. Very quickly, though, the patient experiences the hospital very differently, and realizes that the information that was given to them about life in the hospital has had the effect of reducing the resistance to entering it. Thus, the patient may feel ‘conned’, and these significant figures can function as part of a betrayal funnel.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.
Capps D. The mortification of the self: Erving Goffman’s analysis of the mental hospital. Pastoral psychology. 2016 Feb 1;65(1):103-26.

questions.question_text: Of the following, the life event with the highest rating on the Holmes and Rahe scale is
questions.explanation:
In 1967, psychiatrists Thomas Holmes and Richard Rahe examined over 5000 patients’ medical records to determine whether stressful events cause illnesses. Patients ranked a list of 43 life events based on a relative score. Each event had a different ‘weight’ for stress. Their results were published as the Social Readjustment Rating Scale, now commonly known as the Holmes and Rahe Stress Scale. The scale lists common stressful events and arbitrarily assigns a value of 50 Life Change Units (LCUs) to the stress caused by marriage. Death of a spouse has the highest LCUs at 100, followed by divorce (73 LCUs), and marital separation (65 LCUs).
Ref: Noone PA. The Holmes–Rahe Stress Inventory. Occupational Medicine. 2017 Oct 1;67(7):581-2.
Holmes TH, Rahe RH. The social readjustment rating scale. Journal of psychosomatic research. 1967.

questions.question_text: Which of the following research materials is covered by the Helsinki Declaration?
questions.explanation:
The World Medical Association (WMA) has developed the Declaration of Helsinki as a statement of ethical principles for medical research involving human subjects, including research on identifiable human material and data. Adopted by the WMA’s General Assembly in 1964, it is the most important set of guidelines about research on human participants. It both reflects and shapes the ethos of international research ethics. It is a living instrument and is reviewed and revised regularly. Its latest revision was in 2013.
Ref: https://www.wma.net/policies-post/wma-declaration-of-helsinki-ethical-principles-for-medical-research-involving-human-subjects/ Malik AY, Foster C. The revised Declaration of Helsinki: cosmetic or real change?. Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine. 2016 May;109(5):184-9.

questions.question_text: A 45 year old man holds out his arm to allow measurement of blood pressure as soon as the staff nurse walks towards him following the daily routine of medication dispensing. Which of the following is true?

options.text: As the patient is competent consent is not needed
Explicit consent is not required as this is a situation of necessity
Explicit consent need not be sought for routine procedures
Blood pressure is measured under principle of best interests

questions.explanation:
Consent may be implied (i.e. the patient does not object to, and cooperates with, the procedure) or may be express (i.e. oral or written permission is explicitly asked for and recorded, often on a detailed consent form). Generally, express (or explicit) consent is obtained for non-trivial or invasive procedures, and for some interventions (e.g. operations), it is mandatory. In contrast, implied consent is assumed here.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 937.
